summary: A flip-chip sensing technique enables fabrication-free measurement of microwave losses in target materials by placing them above a sensor chip with superconducting resonators separated by SU-8 pillars, avoiding processing-induced damage that confounds traditional resonator fabrication. Applied to Ge/SiGe heterostructures and superconducting films, the method reveals that bare Ge and composition-graded SiGe virtual layers exhibit loss tangents of $(183 ± 37) × 10^{-6}$ and $(200 ± 29) × 10^{-6}$, respectively, with HF treatment reducing the as-grown Ge/SiGe QW heterostructure loss from $(658 ± 464) × 10^{-6}$ to $(108 ± 18) × 10^{-6}$.
motivation: Microwave resonators on planar Ge heterostructures show high losses that limit superconductor-semiconductor hybrid quantum devices, but disentangling contributions from substrate, dielectrics, superconductors, and interfaces requires extensive fabrication that introduces confounding damage.
method: A sensor chip with eight $λ/4$ CPW resonators (fabricated from Ta/Nb on Si) and 4 µm SU-8 pillars is flip-chip bonded to target materials; electromagnetic field penetration into the target allows measurement of participation ratios and loss extraction via normalized subtraction from a vacuum baseline, with sensitivity tunable by pillar height from $0.67\%$ to $6.39\%$ for Ge dielectrics and $0.63 × 10^{-6}$ to $14.8 × 10^{-6}$ for superconductor surface oxides.
result: PtSiGe exhibits high microwave loss $(173 ± 130) × 10^{-6}$ that worsens with aging to $(736 ± 134) × 10^{-6}$ after two months, limiting its use as a standalone superconductor; Nb coating (Nb-PtSiGe) reduces loss to $(11.1 ± 1.9) × 10^{-6}$ with lower aging sensitivity, while raising transport critical temperature nearly three-fold from $0.54$ K to $1.5$ K, though both films show reduced RF critical temperature $(T_C^{\mathrm{RF}} ≈ 0.31–0.32$ K) indicating gap inhomogeneity.
